scope.note: Client-to-host direction only. Host-to-client *Result types are authored by the host, so they disclose nothing the host did not already have. This file records what an untrusted host can OBSERVE; it is not an integrity model, so who may forge a field is out of scope except for the `signed` annotation.

excludedSurfaces.reason: Group chat is outside the package scope of the write-up; these entries would have no table row to map to, which would hollow out the unmapped-is-a-failure rule.

Device registration and runtime-auth state. Host-visible and real, but the write-up models the inbox and storage components; these entries would have no table row to map to, which would hollow out the unmapped-is-a-failure rule. Enumerating it is its own work.

engineAndFrontEnds.reason: The core engine, its FFI surface, and the CLI and desktop front ends. Their types are commands, events, effects and view models; whatever of theirs reaches a host does so by being one of the wire types, never by being serialized itself.

localState.reason: Client state, in memory or in the local store. Serialized to disk behind the passphrase-derived key, never to a host; Corrupt is where the write-up accounts for it.

mlsBoundary.reason: The MLS library boundary. What crosses it is RFC 9420's wire format, which the write-up assumes rather than models; the only part of it a host sees is the wrapped frame in Envelope.bytes, enumerated there.

support.reason: Signature framing, error plumbing, logging, filesystem helpers, outbound fetch, and this checker itself. Nothing here defines a type that is serialized anywhere.

nonSyntacticLeakage.note: Doubled by the R1 rotation change; recorded there as a traffic-pattern cost. Also directly readable today from PrivateMessage.content_type and epoch; after the R3 wrap only size class remains.
PrivateMessage.epoch and content_type are cleartext in every frame and identical at both inboxes; not a sentinel so not caught by Check X. Removed by the R3 frame wrap.
Records are deleted only at retention expiry, not on ack, so the host holds every envelope header for 30 days past delivery.
Already carried by the Linkability row as `sender address`. The network layer is not addressable here, so application-layer anonymity is the ceiling of any repair in this component.

limits: Containment is not information. This checks for a sentinel SUBSTRING, so any leak that is a FUNCTION of a secret - a hash, a size bucket, a first byte, a few bits of tag - passes clean. This limit has already bitten once, and not in the way it was written: the prediction named hashing conversation_id as the trigger, while what actually happened is that R3 made it random, after which every field carrying it reported clean. The repair was to capture the generated value as a sentinel, which works only because one value is shared across the fixtures; it does nothing for a genuine hash.
Non-syntactic channels are not modelled at all; see nonSyntacticLeakage, where checked:false records that their absence is a decision and not an oversight.

`fate` uses the Fate column's vocabulary, but nothing here checks that the write-up actually assigns that fate. CI proves a human recorded a decision in a coordinate system the write-up cannot silently rename, not that the two agree. That reconciliation is still by hand, and it is deliberately the only coupling: a generator that rendered these entries into a table the write-up did not read was deleted rather than repaired.

Inhabitation (bits) is declared, not yet measured. `constant` and `absent` claims are reviewed by hand until an engine-driven corpus check lands; the structural path set and the carries sets ARE measured.

Compile-time exhaustiveness has holes: serde(flatten), a serde_json::Value-typed field, serde(untagged), or a non-exhaustive match elsewhere would each make these checks go quiet rather than red. None are present in the in-scope types today.

Widening `carries` to silence a red check is still a one-line edit to this file. The generator that made such a widening show up in a published artifact is gone; its replacement is the partition test of the engine-driven corpus, which measures `carries` instead of reading it. Until that lands, this file is trusted where it asserts and checked only where it can be contradicted.

lane and mid are not sentinels, deliberately. Both are random per-conversation or per-message values, so within one execution they behave like the conversation sentinel and would report where they are carried — but the claim worth testing about a lane is that the two inboxes of one conversation share no token, and that needs a corpus with both sides in it. Adding them against a single-inbox fixture would produce a green that means nothing. Deferred to the engine-driven corpus.

The group-outbox spill keys are assembled inline at services/cloudflare/src/group-outbox/service.ts, not through leakage-keys.ts, so the TS check that every minted template is recorded here cannot see them. This is the same failure the module partition on the Rust side closed, one level down: a key built at a call site is invisible to a check that reads the builders. Not repaired in this round, because repairing it means deciding whether the group-outbox surface enters the enumeration at all, and scope.excludedSurfaces currently says it does not.

welcome-pickup is the one object named by a digest rather than by a fresh random: it is pure R2 with no Durable Object beside it, so the name has to be one both sides recompute from the capability the fetcher presents. The builder therefore does not itself guarantee the name carries nothing — the caller does, by passing a hash.

entries.note: Wrapped MLS frame (nonce || ChaCha20-Poly1305). Check X must stay empty, and since the fixture frame now carries the shared conversation sentinel in its PrivateMessage group_id, an empty result is evidence that the wrap hides the frame header rather than an artefact of the id being random. Unwrapping it would report conversation.

An opaque key: a namespace and a fresh 256-bit name. It used to name the sending user, the device, the conversation and the message, and the conversation segment was identical at both ends — a token shared across the two inboxes of one conversation, which is exactly what the per-direction lanes and the frame wrap existed to remove. Routing needs the reference; it never needed any of that.
Random opaque id minted by the inbox (`request:{randomOpaqueId()}`), the host's own handle for a queued first contact. It carries nothing about the sender.

The admission credential, and the quota partition. A 1:1 payload is placed in the recipient runtime, which admits the sender on the same lane it admits its envelopes on; revoking the contact deletes one key and stops both.
The destination URL. It names the recipient device because that is the inbox being addressed, which is the same thing the append request line already discloses.

A per-lane counter starting at 1, returned as the append `seq` while a lane is still queued, where an admitted lane returns the device-global head. The write-up's Send says the inbox answers with a sequence number and nothing else; that is false while the two counters differ, so the sender reads its own admission state off the first reply.
Accepted-lane buckets. Unknown lanes share rate-limit:first-contact.
Holds the list of first-contact lanes that have attempted contact.

A fresh 256-bit name. Read access was always gated on an independent capability, so the identifiers this key used to carry bought nothing and cost a cross-inbox token: the same key reached the recipient inbox as envelope.storageRef.ref, and its conversation segment was identical at both ends.
A fresh 256-bit name; the inbox records it on the record index, so nothing has to re-derive it.
Served unauthenticated, so anyone who has ever seen a share link can re-fetch the current append capability indefinitely.
Named by the SHA-256 of the pickup capability: pure R2 with no Durable Object beside it, so the name has to be one both sides recompute. Group scope, but it shares the single bucket.
InboxRecord with the four-field envelope; sender identifiers are no longer in the header.
Random request id; no longer request:{senderUserId}.

protectedFields.note: app:{conversation_id}:{nonce}:{sender_device_id}. Nothing in the host view carries it; the earlier claim that the header duplicated it was left over from a header that no longer exists.
Random 128-bit local MLS group_id; no longer duplicated on the 1:1 envelope header.

The 1:1 envelope header has not named the sender since the header shrank to four fields. Until the object key became opaque this still reached the host through envelope.storageRef.ref, which is why it was recorded as duplicated rather than confidential — a claim about a header that no longer held it.
Same as sender_user_id, and transitively worse: a device id names its user.
Transitively: the header carries recipient_device_id, and a device id is format!("device:{user_fp}:{device_fp}"), so it already names the user.
Fan-out width is deliberately hidden; the header names one recipient device.

group.reason: Group chat is outside the package scope of the write-up.

hostToClient.reason: Authored by the host; discloses nothing it did not have.

deferred.reason: The identity-publication and runtime-auth surface. Real and host-visible, but a distinct surface that R3 does not touch; enumerating it is its own piece of work. Listed here so a NEW type still fails the partition guard.

localOnly.reason: Never serialized to a host. ProtectedAppMessage is covered separately by protectedFields.

insideTheWrap.reason: The plaintext of a wrapped direct frame. These are serialized, but into the AEAD that Envelope.bytes carries, so a host sees only ciphertext — the evidence is that append_request.envelope.bytes measures an empty carries set while the fixture frame embeds the conversation sentinel. Worth naming rather than folding into localOnly: DirectCommitProof puts sender_user_id and sender_device_id back inside the frame, under a second signature domain, which is a partial reversal of the decision that removed sender_proof. It is safe where it sits and it is not in the write-up; whether it can be removed is an open question, not an oversight.
